item.content:encoded:
SANTA MONICA, Calif., Sept. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Los Angeles-based car shopping site Edmunds today announced it is fueling Los Angeles Dodgers fans for October baseball with $25,000 in free gas on Friday, September 25.
Edmunds is joining forces with Dodgers fan-favorite #25 Tommy ‘Tanks’ Edman for the Tommy Tanks Gas Giveaway at Longo Lexus in El Monte, CA. Fans must arrive by car to participate and are encouraged to wear Dodger blue attire. A total of 333 $75 gas gift cards from 76® will be distributed while supplies last, limited to one per vehicle.
With Edman and the team away for their final regular season series in San Francisco, Dodgers fans are invited to root on the Boys in Blue as they gear up for October baseball.
Taking ‘Tommy Tanks’ Beyond the Ballpark with $25K in Free Gas
Playing off Edman’s No. 25, Edmunds will give away $25,000 in gas on September 25, bringing his ‘Tommy Tanks’ moniker beyond the ballpark and to the pump for LA drivers.
- Date: Friday, September 25
- Time: 6 - 8 PM
- Location: Longo Lexus in El Monte, CA (3530 Peck Rd, El Monte, CA 91731)
- How to Participate: Fans must arrive by car and enter Longo Lexus through the main entrance on Peck Road; walk-up entry is not permitted. One person per vehicle will receive a wristband before parking and heading to the Longo Lexus showroom to complete a quick form, engage with the Tommy Tanks Gas Calculator, and receive the gift card. Dodgers gear is encouraged! A total of 333 $75 gas gift cards from 76® will be available while supplies last, limited to one per vehicle.
- More Information: Full event details and giveaway rules can be found at edmunds.com/freegas.
VIDEO: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/r6zzAd3Iqtk
Dodgers Fans Said They’d Turn Down $1 Gas for Another Championship. Edmunds is Fueling Their Dedication.
The Tommy Tanks Gas Giveaway was inspired by a survey of more than 2,000 Dodgers fans conducted by Edmunds earlier this season1 that revealed just how far fans are willing to go for the Boys in Blue. When asked to choose between the Dodgers winning a third consecutive World Championship or gas prices falling to $1 per gallon, 80% chose another ring. And they’re willing to brave some serious LA traffic for their team, too: Nearly one-third (32%) said they’d spend five hours or more traveling to and from a Dodgers home game in October.
“Between driving in LA traffic and keeping up with high fuel costs, local drivers could use a win,” said Tommy Edman. “Teaming with Edmunds to fuel up the best fanbase in baseball for another October run is an awesome way to thank LA for showing up for us night in and night out.”
High Gas Prices Add to Affordability Pressures for LA Drivers
The giveaway comes as LA drivers continue to face stubbornly high prices at the pump, adding to the persistent affordability challenges facing vehicle owners. According to AAA, the average price for regular fuel in the Los Angeles/Long Beach metro area was $6.09 yesterday, September 16.
The pressure at the pump comes as consumers are already navigating record-high vehicle expenses: Edmunds recently reported that the average monthly payment on new-vehicle purchases hit a new record of $777 in Q2, and the average price for a 3-year-old used vehicle rose to $32,461 last quarter, a new second-quarter record.
“We know how much Southern Californians rely on their cars and how quickly the costs of driving can add up,” said Alison Steinlauf Anziska, senior vice president of marketing at Edmunds. “Dodgers fans have shown us just how far they’ll go to support their team, and Tommy’s been showing them exactly why they call him ‘Tommy Tanks.’ We thought it would be fun to take that nickname beyond the ballpark and give fans a little relief at the pump as they cheer on the Dodgers into October.”
More Dodgers Fan Survey Findings Highlight Serious Dedication
Beyond their willingness to choose another Dodgers championship over $1 gas and spend long hours on the road traveling to October home games, Edmunds’ survey of more than 2,000 Dodgers fans from earlier this season revealed a few other ways their fandom shows up on and off the road:
- Many fans are susceptible to catching a case of the ‘Dodger blues’: Two-thirds (66%) of fans said they have skipped work, school or another major obligation to attend a Dodger game.
- Dodgers passion extends to the driveway: 13% of Dodger fans drive a blue car, well above the California state average of 7% of new vehicles sold in 2025.
- Fuel economy matters to Dodgers fans: When considering the car-shopping priorities that mattered most to fans, fuel economy ranked among the top three factors, along with price and reliability.
Edmunds, Edman and the Dodgers Go ‘Back-to-Back’
The gas giveaway and fan survey are the latest elements of Edmunds’ ‘Back to Back’ brand campaign in collaboration with the Dodgers and Edman. As part of the campaign, Edmunds is also transforming its Gas Savings Calculator into the ‘Tommy Tanks Gas Calculator,’ helping consumers estimate how much they could save on fuel by switching to a more fuel-efficient vehicle or different powertrain.
Earlier this season, Edmunds executed a sweepstakes offering fans a chance at the ultimate VIP gameday experience and a free vehicle appraisal. Edmunds also launched ‘The Challenge,’ the brand’s second consecutive hero digital ad campaign starring Edman as he helps fans make the right call in their next car shopping decision with the help of Edmunds.
For more information and official rules, check out the Tommy Tanks Gas Giveaway event page at edmunds.com/freegas.
1 *Source: Edmunds survey of Dodgers fans, n=2,071, April 2026
About Longo Lexus
Longo Lexus, located in El Monte, California, is a premier Lexus dealership dedicated to delivering exceptional guest experiences throughout every stage of the vehicle ownership journey. Part of Penske Motor Group, Longo Lexus has been recognized as the #1 Lexus dealership for new vehicle sales in the Western United States since opening in 1990. The dealership offers an extensive selection of new, L/Certified, and pre-owned vehicles, supported by state-of-the-art service, parts, collision repair, and in-house customization facilities. Built on a longstanding commitment to integrity, excellence, and putting guests first, Longo Lexus continues to set the standard for luxury automotive retail and ownership. For more information, visit longolexus.com or follow Longo Lexus on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and LinkedIn.
About Edmunds
Edmunds guides car shoppers online from research to purchase. With in-depth reviews of every new vehicle, shopping tips from an in-house team of experts, plus a wealth of consumer and automotive market insights, Edmunds helps millions of shoppers each month select, price and buy a car with confidence. Regarded as one of America's best workplaces by Newsweek, Fortune, Great Place to Work and Built In, Edmunds is based in Santa Monica, California. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are set to wrap up a four-game series on Thursday afternoon with the Cincinnati Reds after dropping Wednesday night’s game 6-2.
Ahead of the finale, however, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts decided to make some sudden changes to his starting lineup, one of which includes veteran star Mookie Betts, who is coming off a three-hit performance.
Dodgers Make Sudden Betts Decision
After hitting in the two-hole on Wednesday and drawing the start at shortstop, Betts is nowhere to be found in Thursday’s starting lineup as Roberts is seemingly giving the veteran the day off.
With that decision, as they gear up to face right-handed pitcher Brady Singer of the Reds, slugger Freddie Freeman will move into the two-hole behind leadoff hitter Tommy Edman, while Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernandez will bat in the three and four spots.
Here’s the full Dodgers lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Dodgers 9/17 T. Edman CF F. Freeman 1B K. Tucker RF T. Hernández LF M. Muncy 3B J. De Paula DH H. Feduccia C A. Freeland 2B M. Rojas SS J. Wrobleski SP.”
Dodgers 9/17
T. Edman CF
F. Freeman 1B
K. Tucker RF
T. Hernández LF
M. Muncy 3B
J. De Paula DH
H. Feduccia C
A. Freeland 2B
M. Rojas SS
J. Wrobleski SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 17, 2026
Looking at Betts’ 2026 Season
In his 13th MLB season and seventh as a member of the Dodgers, Betts has appeared in 114 games and is hitting .250 across 444 at-bats, with 64 runs, 111 hits, 20 home runs, and 62 RBIs while slugging .430 with a .746 OPS.
Dodgers Right Now
Los Angeles is dealing with a few concerning injuries at the moment. Most notably to Shohei Ohtani, but they still enter Thursday having clinched the NL West with a 92-60 overall record.
They’re still looking to secure a top-two seed, which would get them a first-round bye. After wrapping up their series with the Reds, they’ll finish the regular season with series against the San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and then the Giants again.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.
Dodgers Lineup vs. Reds
1. Tommy Edman, CF
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Kyle Tucker, RF
4. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
5. Max Muncy, 3B
6. Josue De Paula, DH
7. Hunter Feduccia, C
8. Alex Freeland, 2B
9. Miguel Rojas, SS
P. Justin Wrobleski, LHP
Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Elly De La Cruz hit a two-run homer and the Cincinnati Reds at least temporarily prevented the Los Angeles Dodgers from clinching the NL West title with a 6-2 victory on Wednesday night.
The Dodgers (92-60) needed a win or a loss by San Diego to win their fifth straight NL West crown and 13th in 14 seasons. The Padres played at Colorado later Wednesday.
Left-hander Blake Snell started for the Dodgers but departed after one inning with left groin tightness. Snell, who threw a no-hitter for the Giants in his last appearance in Great American Ball Park, faced three batters, allowing a hit with a strikeout on 19 pitches.
Blake Treinen took over in the second as the first of six relievers used by Los Angeles.
Mookie Betts singled off Andrew Abbott in the third and scored on Will Smith's double to put the Dodgers ahead 1-0. Abbott allowed a run on three hits with five walks in 4 2/3 innings. Tejay Antone (3-2), the third of six Cincinnati pitchers, got the last out of the sixth.
De La Cruz's homer off Seth Halvorsen (1-2), his 28th of the season, put the Reds ahead 2-1 in the third. It was De La Cruz's fifth longball against the Dodgers this season, most of any opposing player.
Dane Myers' homer off Bobby Miller, his seventh, extended the Reds' lead to 3-1 in the fifth.
Juan Brito's RBI single made it 4-2 in the sixth.
TJ Friedl singled with the bases loaded in the seventh to drive in two runs. Sal Stewart was thrown out at the plate by Dodgers center fielder Tommy Edman to end the inning.
The Dodgers stranded 12 runners and went 0 for 11 with runners in scoring position.
Up next
RHP Brady Singer (6-14, 5.38 ERA) will start Thursday's series finale for the Reds. The Dodgers had not announced their starter.

item.content:encoded:
Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona.
But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself.
"I try to stay positive and bring the same energy that you guys know and see everyday — smiling, making jokes," Hernández told me. "But at the same time, it’s really hard."
(Photo by David Jordan/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts noticed his typically jovial outfielder looking a bit more sullen at times, too. It was understandable.
Hernández, a fixture in the Dodgers’ lineup whose clutch hitting, encouraging nature and penchant for performing on the sport’s biggest stage helped his team win back-to-back World Series titles, had a respectable .785 OPS when he went on the injured list on May 29 with a left hamstring strain.
But the 33-year-old did not look the same when he returned a month later. From June 29 to Aug. 29, his .592 OPS was the ninth-lowest mark among all qualified MLB hitters over that stretch.
"Some of the joy was sucked out," Roberts told me, "because it’s hard to be so joyful when you’re not performing. He was still a good teammate, always a good teammate, but I know there were a lot of frustrating moments for him."
Hernández’s struggles were compounded by the fact that the Dodgers were also getting little from their other corner outfielder, Kyle Tucker, or the rest of an offense that looked lifeless for much of the summer.
But now, at a crucial juncture for his team with All-Stars Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages sidelined, another All-Star in Freddie Freeman battling knee soreness and the playoffs just weeks away, Hernández is taking his frustration out constructively.
He is annihilating the baseball in September, leaving his summer slump behind and giving the Dodgers reason to believe in the depth of their offense again.
"When he catches fire," Dodgers infielder Tommy Edman said, "he’s as good as anybody in the game."
Even among Hernández’s best career stretches, the tear he’s on now stands out. Every part of his offensive profile is enhanced.
Hernández, who’s prone to swing and miss even when he’s going right, is making better swing decisions. From last month to this month, he has lowered his chase rate from 36.7% to 24.8%, tripled his walk rate from 4.3% to 15.1% and cut his strikeout rate nearly in half from 31.2% to 18.9%.
And along with a more selective approach, he is punishing every mistake in a way he couldn’t earlier this season.
Hernández’s hard-hit rate has skyrocketed from 34.5% in July to 47.5% in August to 60% this month. His average exit velocity this September (96.6 mph) is the highest of any month in his career.
Eight of his 10 hardest-hit balls this season have come in the last two weeks, and his power is being generated by the highest average bat speed he has produced in any month over the last two seasons (74.1 mph).
It’s a far cry from where Hernández was just a couple of weeks ago, when his year-long struggle against right-handers had the Dodgers considering using a platoon in left field. That no longer appears to be a consideration.
"Right now," Roberts said, "it’s just night and day."
So how, exactly, did Hernández find his way back?
"The most important part, he’s healthy," Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas told me. "If he’s healthy, we can see the Teo that’s running hard on the bases, stealing bases, going first to third. Obviously the bat is there because it’s his best tool, but seeing the complete player now is really refreshing."
Earlier this season, Hernández’s downturn looked familiar.
A year ago, he had the highest batting average on the team when he went on the IL in May with an adductor strain. He returned two weeks later, then watched his OPS precipitously drop 200 points from May 21 (.927) to July 21 (.727).
Clearly, the lower-body injury had lingered, throwing off his swing and sapping his power.
This year, it was happening again, only with his hamstring. The swing that worked for him before the injury was putting too much pressure on his lower half. Upon his return from the IL, he had a .562 OPS overall in July and a team-worst .496 OPS against right-handed pitching in August.
"I told Dave, ‘If you feel like you have to use somebody else in there, just do it,’" Hernández said.
(Photo by Meg Oliphant/Getty Images)
That would not be necessary. At least, not again after Aug. 25. The decision to sit him that day was noteworthy, considering the Dodgers were coming off an off day and facing a Braves team they were battling for a first-round bye.
In hindsight, it might have served as a wake-up call.
On Aug. 26, Hernández returned to the lineup in Atlanta with a two-hit day. He then ended the Dodgers’ next series in Detroit with a two-run homer off Framber Valdez, which might have been the turning point.
"I think that at-bat gave him the extra life that he needed for the last part of the season," Rojas said. "Obviously, baseball is about confidence, and you find confidence with success, and I thought that’s what he needed. He needed, like, one good swing that he knows he’s back, and then all of a sudden we see the results we get now."
There’s also a mechanical component to Hernández’s upswing.
Too often, Hernández felt both rushed and late at the plate as he worked his way back from his hamstring injury. He has since opened his stance in an effort, he says, to slow his body up, prevent his front hip from flying open and give him more time to see the ball. He has also traded his more subtle toe tap for a slightly more exaggerated leg lift and hip twist as a timing mechanism that seems to be producing more power.
These were moves he used before in his career. Now healthy, he feels his body can withstand the added force once again.
Sometimes with hitting, the littlest tweaks can yield the biggest results.
"That’s why it’s hard," Hernández told me. "One day, you don’t know what you’re doing. The next day, you change barely — sometimes it’s your hands, sometimes it’s your legs, sometimes it’s how low, how tall [in the stance] — and it can click, and you go on a heater."
Even compared to heaters of the past, though, this one is unlike most for Hernández. If September ended today, his 1.211 OPS this month would be the highest mark in any month of his career.
Hernández maintains that his confidence never wavered through the rough patch; that he knew, at some point, things would turn. His teammates shared that belief.
This was the same guy, after all, who homered in every playoff series last season.
(Photo by Melina Pizano/Getty Images)
"The clutch gene and everything that he has in him, the reason why we got him and the reason why we’ve been so good with him in the lineup the last couple years, nothing changed this year just because of a bad stretch," Rojas told me. "To be honest with you, I was never concerned about it … I want nobody in a big at-bat more than Teo."
After the big hit last month in Detroit, Hernández returned home, made the swing changes and provided the elusive clutch hit the scuffling Dodgers’ offense had been missing with a walk-off double to salvage a series against the Cardinals.
That hit helped spark an eight-game winning streak for the Dodgers, who started to look like themselves again.
Their ebullient left fielder is looking that way, too.
"I feel really good right now," Hernández said. "I’ve been working really hard for this, and I’m glad and happy that everything is coming together."

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.
Dodgers Starting Lineup
- Tommy Edman, CF
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Will Smith, C
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Teoscar Hernández, DH
- Miguel Rojas, 2B
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Kiké Hernández, 3B
- Alex Call, LF
Josue De Paula, Max Muncy and Alex Freeland are out of the lineup with the left-handed pitcher on the mound.

The game will be broadcast on SportsNet LA and in the MLB app.
The game will be broadcast on the radio on AM570 (in English) and KTNQ 1020 AM (in Spanish).

How did Josue De Paula do for Dodgers vs. Reds on Sept. 15?
Josue De Paula made his first start as the Los Angeles Dodgers' leadoff hitter on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
He went 0-for-5 at the plate in the Dodgers' 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds.
The 21-year-old designated hitter jumped up into the leadoff spot in place of Tommy Edman, who was originally in the role after Shohei Ohtani's injury woes.
De Paula added to the Dodgers' offense in a game against the Miami Marlins, hitting a three-run home run for his first career homer on Sept. 13.
The 21-year-old De Paula made his major-league debut for the team at LoanDepot Park on Friday, Sept. 11, becoming the youngest Dodgers player since Alex Verdugo on Sept. 2, 2017.
De Paula has been viewed as the organization's top prospect and recently became the first Dodgers position player called up from AA, while skipping AAA, since Steve Sax in 1981.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”
De La Cruz had another hit, a single in the ninth inning that put runners on the corners for the Reds with no outs. Tanner Scott struck out Sal Stewart, Jose Trevino and Eugenio Suarez to close out the shutout.

item.content:encoded:
Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. He'll get the start tonight, while the Dodgers will counter with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
First pitch in GABP is set for 6:40 PM ET. Here's how both teams will line up:

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– With his already career-worst season reaching nightmarish new depths, Kyle Tucker was pulled aside recently by Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
The topic of conversation: The $240 million outfielder’s playing time over the rest of the season.
Externally, of course, calls had been mounting for Tucker to be platooned, if not outright benched, as his numbers continued to plummet amid an ongoing second-half slump.
Internally, however, the Dodgers had decided to double down on their faith in this offseason’s marquee free-agent signing.
Thus, the message Roberts delivered was simple.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts shared this weekend.
In that exact phrasing?
“I did,” Roberts joked. “That was my young term phrase.”
On this day, Roberts had reason to laugh. The previous two games, Tucker had finally offered signs of life at the plate, posting back-to-back performances with three hits and a home run. Over the last week, Dodgers hitting coaches believed they had finally found a breakthrough with the left-handed slugger’s swing, one that (at least temporarily) cleaned up some mechanical flaws that had hampered him all year.
Alas, in Tucker’s 2026 campaign, no turnaround was ever going to be that simple.
Over the two games since, he has gone 0-for-8 again, including a strikeout with the bases loaded in the top of the ninth on Sunday. On the season, his numbers remain unthinkably disappointing, with a batting average of .226, an OPS of .692 and an almost negligible 0.3 mark in wins above replacement.
At this point, it is all adding up to a lost season for the 29-year-old, who is threatening to become one of the biggest free-agent flops in at least the sport’s recent high-priced history.
And yet, the Dodgers aren’t wavering from their commitment to keep playing the four-time All-Star, rolling the dice “talent level” and “proven track record,” as Roberts cited, by keeping him in the lineup for the long haul.
“I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
The only caveat Roberts offered: “I guess, to that same point, until you can’t, right?”
Trying to identify the root cause of Tucker’s dismal season has been about as easy as discerning his emotions through his stoic and reserved facade.
The one thing everyone has agreed on: “It’s purely mechanical,” as co-hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc told the California Post recently. “His swing plane is pretty unique, but it’s just not working the way that it used to.”
The problem, as Tucker himself conceded last month, has been finding an answer or adjustment that works.
“I feel like I’ve tried just about everything,” he said. “And every time I feel like I’m turning a corner, I get hit with a roadblock.”
Tucker’s swing has always been atypical, both in the way he “lays the bat back” in his stance (which, according to fellow hitting coach Aaron Bates, leads to a longer path in which “his margin for error is a little smaller”) and how he strides through the ball (launching off his back foot with an almost Scottie Scheffler-esque follow-through).
When it’s all synced up, it makes him one of the most consistent hitters in the game; reminiscent to some evaluators of a modern-day Ted Williams.
But when it’s not…
“I think it’s a slippery slope,” Bates said.
Only now, the Dodgers are hoping they have found a way to potentially end the slide.
For much of the year, Bates said Tucker was struggling to replicate his old, inside-out swing path. Instead, he was “cutting down and across the ball,” preventing him from squaring up heaters or adjusting to off-speed pitches. According to MLB’s Statcast system, his rate of “barreled” balls has fallen almost in half as a result, from 10.8% last year (and 12.9% in 2024) to 6.3% this season.
Their initial attempt at a fix was having Tucker cycle through old drills and mental cues he had used in his career previously. Only this time, those old band-aids failed to make a difference, leaving a player who once always had offensive answers toiling with only growing mechanical questions.
Why that is still confounds the Dodgers. Theories have ranged from a slow adjustment to his new surroundings, to potential lingering side effects from the hand fracture he played through last season with the Chicago Cubs.
“It definitely seems like things kind of shifted after [that],” Van Scoyoc said, noting that Tucker also struggled down the stretch in 2025. “So it could be that, but it might not be. We don’t exactly know.”
What was clear was the need to try something different. Thus, there has been constant trial-and-error in Tucker’s elongated batting-cage sessions of late.
Last week, something finally clicked. As Bates described it, Tucker found comfort with the thought of a “no-roll swing” –– where instead of flipping his hands at the end of his follow-through, he keeps them more square to the big part of the field.
“Guys who throw right-handed but hit lefty, it’s something they struggle with sometimes, because the right side of their body is the dominant side,” Bates said, noting that the team has made similar adjustments with Tommy Edman, Alex Freeland and Dalton Rushing this season.
In Tucker’s case, the cue helped flatten his swing.
“He was missing pitches he thought he needed to get on top of,” Bates said, “and needed to think about swinging high instead of swinging down.” It has also kept his barrel in the zone longer, allowing him to re-adjust to off-speed offerings (one of his great strengths as a hitter for most of his career) while better squaring mistakes left over the plate (like the hanging inside sweeper he belted for a grand slam on Friday).
“There’s a lot more room for error hitting the ball, because you can hit it deep and go the other way or catch it out in front and pull it a little bit more,” Tucker explained. “Just trying to be consistent with that and be as long through the zone as possible.”
Whether it proves to be a genuine breakthrough, or just another false start in a season that’s never gotten going, the Dodgers are willing to keep taking the time to find out.
After all, while Tucker’s regular season is beyond salvaging, Van Scoyoc maintained that “he can find it in one swing and then go on a run.”
Thus, they will “ride or die” with him the rest of the way, despite the dismal struggles the last five months have wrought.
“I mean, the numbers probably are what they are, but we’ve got a lot of important games coming next month,” Tucker said, eyeing what he hopes will be validation in the playoffs. “That’s the most important thing … As long as you win the game and kind of contribute to that in some way, that’s all you can really try and do.”
Added Roberts: “If you perform at the right time, all is forgotten.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are one win away from clinching a National League playoff berth.
Monday, September 14, the Dodgers begin a three-game series against the Cincinnati Reds for the second time seven games.
Ahead of tonight’s game, the Dodgers make a couple changes in their lineup, one of them involving utility player Tommy Edman.
Tommy Edman is Back in the Lineup vs. the Reds After a Rest Day on Sunday
Per Los Angeles Dodgers reporter David Vassegh, the team announced their starting lineup against the Cincinnati Reds on Monday.
#Dodgers Lineup vs #Reds LHP, Nick Lodolo: Edman CF, Betts SS, Smith C, Tucker RF, T. Hernandez LF, Rojas 2B, Muncy 3B, E. Hernandez 1B, JDP DH, Tarik Skubal SP,” Vassegh wrote on X.
Edman sat out in Sunday’s loss against the Miami Marlins because Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, did not want him playing all three games on a turf field.
“#Dodgers Dave Roberts originally said Josue De Paula would DH all 3 games in Miami,” Dodgers insider Bill Plunket wrote on X ahead of Sunday’s game. “Thought it thru and decided he didn’t want Teoscar Hernandez or Tommy Edman to play all 3 games on turf here. So De Paula gets the start in LF.”
Edman and the Dodgers have been carefully monitoring the center fielder’s ankle, after spending nearly half the season on the injured list. The 31-year-old underwent an offseason ankle surgery and did not return to the Dodgers lineup until June 17.
While the Dodgers primary center fielder Andy Pages, remains on the injured list, Edman has spent most of starts in center.
Despite slashing .257/.339/.390 in 72 games, Edman’s seven game stretch shows signs of a quite the slump.
He’s batting .091 with five strikeouts, two hits, and two RBIs in his last 22 at-bats. Both of hits coming against the Washington Nationals on September 6.
Hopefully yesterday’s much needed rest day gets Edman back where he needs to be.
Los Angeles Dodgers Magic Number to Win NL West is Four
There only 15 days until the first MLB postseason game, and 13 games left in the season for the Dodgers. They can clinch a postseason berth tonight with a win against the Reds.
“LAD can clinch a postseason berth today with a win at Cincinnati *or* losses by both the Padres (@ COL) AND the Diamondbacks (v. MIA),” Dodgers beat writer Katie Woo wrote on X.
For the National League West, the Dodgers’ magic number is four.
After their series concludes against the Reds, the Dodgers are strictly facing NL West opponents. Two series at-home against the San Francisco Giants and San Diego Padres, and rounding off the season on the road to face San Francisco for the final time in 2026.

item.description:
Tommy Edman is not in the Dodgers’ starting lineup for Sunday’s series finale against the Marlins in Miami.
Edman has been a fixture atop the Dodgers’ lineup since Shohei Ohtani was shelved, so he’ll get a well-deserved day off in this one. Miguel Rojas will cover second base in his absence and will hit eighth against Marlins’ right-hander Eury Perez.
